Triggers.value: A specific texture associated with the event

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad
try hard not think about the trauma
I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event

Memory.value: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.

vignette: Elias remembered the day the department store's upper walkway gave way. The structural failure was man-made, the result of overloaded beams that buckled under the crowd. He had been on the ground floor when the dust hit, but the panic carved the event into his mind. When shoppers surged toward failing exits, Elias felt a crushing weight of bodies pressing against his ribs, a physical proximity so absolute he could not breathe. Worse was the moral violation: people shoved past a fallen man without breaking stride, their indifference stark against his frantic calls. The disaster left him with a handful of frozen snapshots, each moment a high-definition picture. Over time, those images refused to fade. They felt more real than ordinary memories, pressing against his awareness with the weight of ongoing threat. In the months that followed, Elias found his life dictated by the sensory geography of that collapse. At his retail job, the coarse weave of winter coats stacked in the basement warehouse actively reignited the snap-photographs. As the rough fabric sharpened his recall, the sudden flood of dread pushed him toward telling himself the disaster had been minor. This magical thinking became his first line of defense, a deliberate rewriting of reality to blunt the shock. The shame on recall did not stay contained to the stockroom. Whenever the vivid snapshots resurfaced, they cast a long shadow over his present surroundings, making ordinary physical proximity and casual misconduct feel inherently dangerous. Each time those memories rose, he felt a desperate need to silence them. He would retreat to the break room, press his thumb into his palm until the skin bruised, or pick at his fingertips until they bled, using physical pain to drown out the images. Yet the self-harm distraction only worked in fragments. By exhausting himself with the effort to suppress the thoughts, he inadvertently made the trauma feel even more real and immediate. The suppression created a mental vacuum that his brain rushed to fill, leaving the memories more vivid than ever. Over the next year, the painful distraction left him jittery and hyper-alert, which meant the physical proximity of crowded aisles and the texture of rough inventory now spiked his alarm far more quickly. His wife noticed how he flinched when she brushed his shoulder, how he would abruptly leave dinners when conversations grew animated, and how he spent hours staring at the walls. He had come to believe that if he stopped punishing himself for the memories, they would consume him entirely, so he clung to the pain as a tether to control. Eventually, the exhaustion outpaced the coping. Elias stood at the reception desk of the trauma clinic, the brochure worn soft. He was there because the retail environment had become unbearable. He hoped the therapist might help him untangle the shame from the snapshots, to stop the cycle of self-harm that left him shaking. What he feared most was that the memories would remain frozen forever, that the physical proximity of everyday life would always feel like standing inside the collapsing ceiling again. He wanted to believe the disaster was truly over, that he could walk through a crowded store without his body bracing for the next fall.
